content.headline: At least five killed in shooting in Kraków’s main square, police say
content.shortHeadline: At least five killed in Kraków square shooting
content.standfirst: Polish police say a man opened fire from a car in the city’s busy main square and was detained. Authorities are still establishing the number of victims and the circumstances of the attack.

image.caption: Emergency services at the scene of the shooting near Kraków’s main market square.

sources.originalTitle: At least five killed after man opens fire in Krakow square, Polish police say

segments.body: At least five people were killed and around a dozen injured when a man allegedly drove into Kraków’s main market square and fired at people, Polish police said. The suspect was detained after being shot by officers. Police said two officers were among the wounded.

The shooting happened at about 3pm local time on Saturday in Rynek Główny, a popular square that hosts a Christmas market. Authorities urged people to stay away while emergency services responded and investigators worked to establish the full scale and circumstances of the attack.

content.headline: Russian strikes damage Ukraine’s power network ahead of peace talks
content.shortHeadline: Russian strikes hit Ukraine’s power network before talks
content.standfirst: Overnight attacks damaged energy infrastructure and disrupted services in Kyiv and other regions, according to Ukrainian officials. The strikes came days before planned talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the US.

image.caption: Firefighters at the site of a Russian missile attack on Kyiv.

sources.originalTitle: Russian strikes wound nine and damage Ukraine's power network ahead of talks
Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid

segments.body: Russian drones and ballistic missiles struck Ukrainian energy infrastructure overnight, causing power cuts and disrupting electricity, water and heating in parts of Kyiv, Ukrainian officials said. Reports from the BBC and the Guardian differ on the number of people hurt; both describe damage to substations and other infrastructure.

segments.title: Diplomacy under strain
segments.body: Representatives from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet in Abu Dhabi next week. The Guardian reports that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has questioned whether the US-backed discussions can produce results, and says Ukraine and its European partners are wary of proposals touching on European security arrangements.

perspectives.body: The Guardian reports Zelenskyy’s concern that a wider discussion of European-Russian security could be dangerous, and his insistence that Ukraine needs meaningful guarantees before any such debate.

content.headline: New Zealand election leaves parties facing weeks of coalition talks
content.shortHeadline: New Zealand election leaves coalition outcome unclear
content.standfirst: Preliminary results leave no bloc with a clear majority, and special votes could still change the parliamentary balance. A smaller party that crossed the threshold may help determine who governs.

sources.originalTitle: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election

segments.body: Preliminary results from New Zealand’s election show the centre-right National Party with 42 seats and Labour with 36, with neither able to govern alone. National could form a narrow majority with its current partners, ACT and New Zealand First, if the parties reach an agreement. Labour leader Chris Hipkins has not conceded.

segments.title: A possible kingmaker
segments.body: The Opportunity Party won seven seats and crossed the threshold to enter parliament for the first time. Its leader, Qiulae Wong, says the party is open to working with either bloc. More than 99% of votes have been counted, but special votes remain; the electoral commission is due to announce the official result on 27 November.

The campaign focused on cost of living and unemployment. The two largest parties together received around 60% of the vote, according to the preliminary results. National’s Christopher Luxon says he will lead a caretaker government until final results are confirmed and meaningful negotiations can begin.

content.headline: Jehovah’s Witnesses ease blood rules weeks after a member’s death
content.shortHeadline: Jehovah’s Witnesses ease blood rules after member’s death
content.standfirst: The faith now leaves many decisions about blood components to individual members. Isaac Valdez died after refusing a transfusion under the previous teaching, 23 days before the change was announced.

image.caption: Isaac Valdez’s family says he stood by his religious objection to blood transfusions.

sources.originalTitle: This man refused life-saving treatment because of his religion - days later the rules changed

segments.body: Isaac Valdez, 26, died in August after a brain haemorrhage. His family followed his wishes as a Jehovah’s Witness not to accept a blood transfusion, even when a neurosurgeon said an operation requiring one was the only way to save his life. The faith’s Governing Body announced a change to its teaching 23 days after his death.

segments.title: What the teaching change means
segments.body: The new guidance allows members to decide whether to accept many medical procedures involving donated blood components, including plasma, red blood cells and platelets. The faith’s international spokesperson, Paul Gillies, says whole-blood transfusions remain prohibited and describes the change as a fresh application of biblical principles to modern medicine.

segments.title: Questions over the timing
segments.body: Valdez’s twin brother Jacob, who has left the faith, says he believes Isaac might still be alive if the rule had changed sooner and wants leaders to apologise. Gillies says those concerned deserve to be heard compassionately, but does not explain why the change took so long. The BBC says the number of deaths linked to the former teaching is difficult to establish.

content.headline: Paris climate pact has missed its key goal, but still shapes action
content.shortHeadline: Paris climate pact misses target but still guides action
content.standfirst: Global temperatures have exceeded the agreement’s 1.5C threshold for two years, and the UN’s most optimistic outlook now points to greater warming. Experts remain divided over the process but say it still matters.

image.caption: A wildfire in south-west France, amid growing concern about climate-related fire risk.

sources.originalTitle: What’s the point? Ten years after the Paris treaty, are climate talks getting anywhere?

segments.body: The Paris agreement was intended to limit global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, but temperatures have exceeded that threshold for two years. The UN’s most optimistic estimate now points to warming of about 1.7C to 1.8C. Critics say slow, consensus-based negotiations have failed to match the urgency of the climate crisis.

segments.title: A framework with limits
segments.body: Experts quoted by the Guardian disagree on how much the agreement has achieved, but several argue it remains a shared direction for governments and investors. The article describes initiatives outside the main climate talks, including a group of countries drawing up roadmaps to move away from fossil fuels, and a possible target to increase electricity’s share of final energy use.

content.headline: Three teenagers arrested after suspected sword attack near Gloucester school
content.shortHeadline: Three teenagers arrested after Gloucester sword attack
content.standfirst: A 17-year-old suffered a superficial wound in an incident near a school in Tuffley, police say. The school and a nearby primary academy were locked down as officers searched the area.

image.caption: Police attended the scene near St Peter’s High School in Gloucester.

sources.originalTitle: Three teenagers arrested after 17-year-old injured in Gloucester sword attack

segments.body: Three teenagers from Gloucester have been arrested after a 17-year-old was injured in a suspected sword attack near St Peter’s High School in Tuffley. Police said the wound was believed to have been caused by a sword; another young person was not physically hurt. All three suspects remain in custody for questioning.

Armed police searched the area after the incident on Friday morning, and St Peter’s and Willow Primary Academy went into lockdown. Police said there was not thought to be a wider threat and are seeking witnesses or footage. A woman arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender was released on bail while inquiries continue.

content.headline: Five European leaders urge UK deal on shared electricity market
content.shortHeadline: European leaders press UK for electricity-market deal
content.standfirst: Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Denmark want progress on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market at this month’s summit. Former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier says the wider single market cannot be entered on a pick-and-choose basis.

image.caption: Five European leaders are calling for a UK–EU electricity-market agreement.

sources.originalTitle: Five European leaders call for closer EU-UK ties ahead of Brussels summit
UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC

segments.body: The leaders of five European countries, including Denmark, have urged the UK and EU to agree a path towards Britain’s return to the bloc’s internal electricity market at a summit in Brussels on 20 November. They say closer cooperation could help develop North Sea clean energy and bring more efficient electricity trading.

segments.title: The terms of closer ties
segments.body: The Guardian reports that a deal could require a UK contribution to EU cohesion funds, a point of concern for British officials. Separately, former Brexit negotiator Michel Barnier told the BBC that the UK could not rejoin the single market on selected terms: members would have to accept its rules, including the four freedoms.

perspectives.body: Barnier’s warning centres on the single market as a whole: he says access would require the UK to accept the movement of goods, services, capital and people, rather than choose among them.

content.headline: EU citizens sue Home Office over withdrawal of settled-status rights
content.shortHeadline: EU citizens challenge Home Office status decisions
content.standfirst: Campaign group the3million is asking the High Court to rule that the Home Office acted unlawfully when it removed rights from almost 1,500 people granted pre-settled status. The department says it cannot comment while proceedings are under way.

sources.originalTitle: Home Office sued after stripping almost 1,500 EU citizens of right to live in UK

segments.body: Campaign group the3million has lodged a High Court claim over Home Office decisions to tell almost 1,500 EU citizens that their pre-settled status was granted in error. The group says people were stripped of some or all rights without safeguards required under the Brexit withdrawal agreement, including an appeal and an assessment of proportionality.

segments.title: Why some decisions are disputed
segments.body: The cases include people with Italian citizenship by descent who were told they lacked the right status because they had not shown an Italian passport when they applied. The Home Office accepted in October that evidence of Italian citizenship obtained through descent can establish citizenship from birth. The department declined to comment on the court proceedings.

The campaign group is seeking a declaration that the policy is unlawful. It argues that the settlement scheme’s use of evidential flexibility and discretionary decisions left some people unable to know why their status was granted or later challenged. The Home Office has previously faced a successful legal challenge over rights under the withdrawal agreement.

content.headline: Burnham says rape complainants must not feel they are on trial
content.shortHeadline: Burnham says rape complainants must not feel on trial
content.standfirst: The prime minister says he will examine how rape trials are conducted after criticism of arguments heard in Russell Brand’s case. A former Conservative MP and barrister disputes the police chief’s concern about how juries are directed.

sources.originalTitle: Victims in rape cases must not feel like they are on trial, Burnham says

segments.body: Andy Burnham says the government should look closely at how rape trials are conducted so complainants do not feel they are on trial themselves. His comments follow Metropolitan Police chief Sir Mark Rowley’s view that reported arguments in Russell Brand’s trial came close to victim-blaming. Brand was convicted of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

segments.title: Debate over jury guidance
segments.body: Rowley supports a legal duty for judges to direct juries on rape myths and misconceptions. Victims’ Commissioner Claire Waxman and Centre for Women’s Justice founder Harriet Wistrich also argue that jurors need guidance on how people may respond to sexual violence. Burnham says he will study the case but the BBC understands there are no current plans to change the law.

Former Conservative MP and barrister Anna Soubry says judges already give firm directions on these issues and warned that the public is being misled by Rowley’s comments. The different views underline the unresolved debate over how to support complainants while preserving the role of juries.

content.headline: UK plans for a major blackout face questions over backup systems
content.shortHeadline: UK blackout preparations face questions over backup systems
content.standfirst: Lancaster’s 2015 power cut showed how electricity failures can disrupt water, transport and communications. Officials say the grid is resilient, but experts question whether the UK is keeping enough independent ways to communicate.

image.caption: The government’s “Be Ready” campaign advises households on preparing for emergencies.

sources.originalTitle: What happens if all the lights go out? This is the plan for a 'Black Sky' event

segments.body: A flood-related power cut in Lancaster in 2015 left 61,500 people without electricity and disrupted heat, water, transport, shops and cash machines. FM radio and copper-wire landlines continued to work. The episode is used as a warning about a wider “Black Sky” emergency affecting essential services.

segments.title: Resilience and its gaps
segments.body: The BBC says it is preparing an emergency radio service that could operate for at least three days without internet access. The government is also funding high-altitude aircraft intended to provide emergency mobile and internet connectivity. Civil contingency experts warn that water, sewage and emergency communications can depend on electricity.

The government says the UK has one of the world’s most resilient electricity systems and has never experienced a complete grid outage. But a Lancaster professor involved in reviewing the 2015 incident argues that switching off the public copper telephone network risks removing a useful fallback. The landline system is due to be switched off on 31 January 2027.

content.headline: Public EV charging network lacks uniform cyber security protections
content.shortHeadline: UK public EV chargers lack uniform cyber protections
content.standfirst: A Department for Transport consultation proposes security rules for new public chargers, but existing points would not have to be upgraded. Experts warn that attacks could disrupt drivers and public services.

sources.originalTitle: EV security fears as chargers at risk of Russia attack

segments.body: The UK’s public electric-vehicle charging network has no uniform cyber-security requirements, according to Department for Transport documents cited by the i Paper. The government is consulting on protections for new public chargers, including secure updates and safeguards against unauthorised access; existing points would not have to be retrofitted.

segments.title: Potential knock-on effects
segments.body: Researchers and security specialists say attackers could disable chargers, interfere with payment systems or redirect drivers to the same charging point. Disruption could affect buses, ambulances and other services as well as motorists. The extent and consequences of any attack would depend on how many systems were affected and how they were connected.

content.headline: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show’s cancellation
content.shortHeadline: Cast react as Married at First Sight UK is cancelled
content.standfirst: Some former participants welcomed Channel 4’s decision after allegations by cast members, while others say it leaves unanswered questions. Only a summary of the broadcaster’s review has been released.

sources.originalTitle: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed

segments.body: Channel 4 has cancelled Married at First Sight UK after a BBC Panorama investigation reported allegations from three former cast members. Two women alleged they were raped by on-screen husbands, and a third alleged a non-consensual sexual act. The men involved have denied the allegations.

segments.title: Questions remain
segments.body: Some former participants told the BBC they were relieved by the decision; others called for accountability and answers about how concerns were handled. Channel 4 says its review found no breach of broadcasting rules in its handling of issues raised at the time, but the review’s full report has not been published.

An Ofcom investigation is ongoing, and Channel 4 bosses are due to appear before a parliamentary committee on 17 November. The BBC reports that the review did not adjudicate on the serious allegations, which remain a matter for the relevant authorities.

content.headline: Eurovision Song Contest Asia begins in Bangkok with 11 countries competing
content.shortHeadline: Eurovision Asia launches in Bangkok with 11 countries competing
content.standfirst: The contest’s first Asian edition brings acts from 11 countries to Bangkok on 14 November. Organisers hope to build a regional event, but questions remain over its audience, voting and how Eurovision’s traditions will travel.

image.caption: Eurovision Song Contest Asia entrants from Bhutan, South Korea and the Philippines.

sources.originalTitle: Eurovision is heading to Asia: here’s what to expect
Eurovision’s Asia experiment gets under way in flamboyant Bangkok

segments.body: The first Eurovision Song Contest Asia final is scheduled for Bangkok on 14 November, with 11 countries competing: Bhutan, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Laos, Malaysia, Mongolia, Nepal, the Philippines, South Korea, Thailand and Vietnam. Organisers say they intend this to be the first of several regional editions. The show will be streamed on Eurovision’s YouTube channel and broadcast in each participating country.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s on-the-ground report finds signs of limited early interest: a week before the final, tickets remained available and the contest’s Asian social-media account had about 65,000 followers. Eurovision scholar Dean Vuletic also warns that the format’s European origins may make it harder to establish elsewhere.

segments.title: A new regional format, familiar questions
segments.body: The format follows the European contest: countries send one act, and a mix of national juries and public votes decides the winner. Viewers elsewhere can vote too, but those votes are pooled into a 12th territory. The winner will not automatically host the following year; organisers say that could be difficult for smaller countries.

segments.title: Traditions may not travel unchanged
segments.body: Organisers say it is too early to know whether bloc voting will emerge. The reporting notes possible regional ties, as well as tensions between Thailand and Cambodia, whose border dispute remains unresolved. Whether the contest’s camp style and queer culture will translate is also uncertain: one expert cautions that participating countries have different laws and media environments.

content.headline: Macklemore says nine US arenas rejected his Palestine benefit tour
content.shortHeadline: Macklemore says nine US arenas rejected his Palestine benefit tour
content.standfirst: The rapper says venues withdrew available dates after learning his planned shows would raise funds for Palestine. His account follows his removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour; the named arenas have not responded in this reporting.

image.caption: Macklemore performs on the Free Palestine tour in Dublin.

sources.originalTitle: Macklemore says that nine US arenas turned down his Free Palestine tour

segments.body: Macklemore says nine major US arenas turned down his proposed Free Palestine benefit tour, including Madison Square Garden, Barclays Center and Crypto.com Arena. In an Instagram post, he alleges that dates initially offered for later this year were taken off the table after venues learned the shows were fundraisers for Palestine. The report includes no response from the arenas.

segments.title: A dispute over the US tour
segments.body: The claims follow Macklemore’s removal from Ed Sheeran’s US tour after the rapper made a speech supporting Palestine. Sheeran said venues had told him they would refuse to host the tour if Macklemore remained as a supporting act. Sheeran also said that choosing not to speak publicly about the conflict did not mean he lacked personal views or concern.

segments.title: Macklemore vows to keep organising
segments.body: Macklemore describes the venue decisions as intimidation and suppression of his political speech, and says he plans to continue organising benefit shows. He points to sold-out European dates in Dublin, Paris and London as evidence of support. The reporting presents his allegations and statements, but does not independently establish why the venues declined.

content.headline: Spice Girls’ 30th-anniversary Singles Collection offers more packaging than new
content.shortHeadline: Spice Girls’ anniversary box set offers little new for fans
content.standfirst: The band’s 30th-anniversary release packages 160 tracks across CDs or vinyl, but most have appeared in earlier reissues. The review finds the collection’s main novelty in a previously unreleased song featuring Victoria Beckham on lead vocals.

image.caption: The Spice Girls during their 1990s heyday.

sources.originalTitle: Spice Girls: The Singles Collection review – stop fleecing your fans right now, thank you very much

segments.body: After social-media teasers raised hopes of a reunion, the Spice Girls announced a box set rather than a tour or documentary. The Singles Collection gathers their singles, B-sides, remixes and demos in a 14-CD set, with a 7-inch vinyl version also available. Its price and the amount of previously repackaged material prompt the review’s central complaint: fans are being asked to pay for an anniversary product with little new music.

segments.title: One archival curiosity stands out
segments.body: The notable unreleased track is “Do You Think About Me,” recorded when the group was still called Touch. Its particular interest, the reviewer says, is Victoria Beckham’s lead vocal: she sounds confident on a song that moves between sweetness and a more forceful delivery. The compilation also collects enjoyable early B-sides, even as the large number of remixes makes the set feel overwhelming.

segments.title: The songs still make the case
segments.body: The critique is of the packaging, not the group’s catalogue. The review highlights the lasting energy of “Wannabe,” “Say You’ll Be There” and “Stop,” along with the band’s ballads. But repeated anniversary releases and merchandise, it argues, risk burying the music beneath another round of products for fans.

content.headline: Wynonna Judd’s new album turns family grief and hardship into song
content.shortHeadline: Wynonna Judd turns grief and hardship into a raw new album
content.standfirst: After a decade without an album, the country singer returns with The Hard Truth, a pared-back record shaped by family loss and personal struggle. She describes making it as part of her healing, with songs that address her mother and daughter directly.

image.caption: Wynonna Judd, whose new album is The Hard Truth.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I went into a deep, deep hole’: Wynonna Judd on overcoming family tragedy and putting a lifetime of love and pain into her new album

segments.body: The Hard Truth is Wynonna Judd’s first album in a decade. She has left behind the polished Nashville sound of earlier work for a rawer blend of country, blues and soul, co-writing nearly every track. Judd says she made the record as an act of healing after years of personal upheaval: “There’s a lot of love and pain on this record,” she says. “It’s very raw and very real.”

segments.title: Songs facing family loss
segments.body: The album addresses Judd’s mother Naomi, who died by suicide in 2022, the day before the Judds were due to be inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame. On “All Downhill from Ashland,” Wynonna sings directly to her mother about the cost of their shared musical life. Another song, “Girl Who Could Sing,” addresses the biological father she learned about as an adult and never had the chance to meet.

segments.title: A difficult present, too
segments.body: Judd also speaks about her adult daughter’s addiction and says she is raising her four-year-old granddaughter. She calls the child a blessing and a reason to face each morning. The interview places these ongoing pressures alongside Judd’s return to music, rather than presenting the album as a neat resolution to grief.

content.headline: Rita Wilson’s new album charts a woman’s life and a late-blooming voice
content.shortHeadline: Rita Wilson finds her voice on a new album about womanhood
content.standfirst: On Sound of a Woman, the actor and songwriter explores ageing, motherhood, illness and self-acceptance. Wilson also reflects on Hollywood’s ageism and why songwriting gave her room to say things her acting roles did not.

image.caption: Rita Wilson, whose album Sound of a Woman is out now.

sources.originalTitle: Rita Wilson: ‘My body turned on me – but it was also there to heal me’

segments.body: Rita Wilson says Sound of a Woman grew from a desire to explore women’s lives, from young love to loss and ageing. Across country-flavoured songs, she writes about body image, motherhood and finding a voice later in life. She began pursuing songwriting in her fifties, after feeling that the acting roles offered to her had become repetitive.

segments.title: Speaking beyond the roles
segments.body: Wilson says Hollywood remains “a very youth-oriented business” and that she once felt nervous about saying so publicly. Songwriting, she explains, gave her a way to express ideas she had not been asked to explore in her acting work. She points to “Spare Keys” as a song about breaking with an old self and allowing a new one to emerge.

segments.title: A song about the body
segments.body: The album also includes “Whose Body Is This?”, which Wilson connects to the changes her body has undergone, including a bilateral mastectomy after breast cancer. She describes the song as an attempt at acceptance and gratitude: her body, she says, was also there to help her heal.

content.headline: Richard Thompson looks back on Fairport Convention’s tragedy and a life in folk
content.shortHeadline: Richard Thompson reflects on Fairport, loss and his new album
content.standfirst: The folk guitarist discusses his 20th solo album, his London musical roots and the 1969 van crash that killed Fairport Convention drummer Martin Lamble and designer Jeannie Franklyn. He says the band did not know how to process the loss.

image.caption: Richard Thompson, the folk guitarist and former Fairport Convention member.

sources.originalTitle: Fairport Convention’s Richard Thompson on the crash that killed his bandmate

segments.body: Richard Thompson has released Hippies, Thugs and Heroes, the latest in a six-decade career that began with Fairport Convention. He says he remains committed to making music that does not sound “overly American,” even though he has lived in the US for much of the past 35 years. His new songs draw on a cast of characters and memories from his past.

segments.title: A loss the band still remembers
segments.body: In 1969, a road accident on the way back from a Birmingham gig killed Fairport drummer Martin Lamble, 19, and Jeannie Franklyn, Thompson’s girlfriend. Thompson, who was in the van, recalls trying to reach Franklyn after the crash. “We did not deal with it,” he says, describing a time when the band had no support mechanism and quickly returned to work.

segments.title: Memory as material
segments.body: Thompson says writing his memoir, Beeswing, prompted him to revisit experiences he had put aside. Some new songs draw on people and places from his life, while others take a more fictional route. He says he is still learning as a musician and is already considering another album and a musical.

content.headline: A Taylor Swift fan remembers discovering her on MySpace in 2006
content.shortHeadline: Before Taylor Swift was famous, a fan found her on MySpace
content.standfirst: Twenty years after Swift’s debut, a former teenage fan recalls the online community that formed around her early songs. The memory traces how direct contact and a sense of shared discovery helped make an unknown country singer feel like a friend.

image.caption: Taylor Swift as a teenage country singer early in her career.

sources.originalTitle: The Taylor Swift I knew on MySpace in 2006

segments.body: The writer first found Taylor Swift through MySpace, after a friend sent a link to the page of a teenage country singer inspired by the Dixie Chicks. In 2006, before Swift’s rise to global stardom, the writer and other young fans traded comments, collected press clippings and waited for the debut album.

segments.title: A sense of being part of it
segments.body: Swift’s blogs, fan interactions and stories about school and life on the road made her seem familiar to the writer and friends. Their enthusiasm became a shared project: they recruited other fans online and treated each radio play or new press mention as a collective milestone. The essay recalls that connection without overlooking the promotional strategy and family support around Swift’s early career.

segments.title: Hearing the songs again
segments.body: The self-titled debut, released in October 2006, turned teenage heartbreak into direct, melodic songs that the writer remembers sharing on profile pages and message statuses. With hindsight, the essay considers how an artist who made young fans feel like outsiders would become one of the world’s biggest musicians, changing expectations of what women songwriters could control in their careers.

content.headline: Bob Dylan’s 1976 Rolling Thunder recordings bring a lost tour into focus
content.shortHeadline: Bob Dylan’s Rolling Thunder Revue gets its 1976 story back
content.standfirst: A 39-disc archive and two full concerts illuminate the spring 1976 leg of Dylan’s Rolling Thunder Revue, long overshadowed by its 1975 predecessor. The review finds a volatile, searching performer in recordings that complicate the tour’s familiar legend.

sources.originalTitle: The Rolling Thunder Revue: The 1976 Live Recordings

segments.body: A new archive gathers professionally recorded material from Bob Dylan’s 1976 Rolling Thunder Revue, including full versions of the Fort Worth and Fort Collins concerts. The release also comes in smaller standalone sets. The review argues that it corrects the impression that the tour’s second run was merely an afterthought to the better-known 1975 shows.

segments.title: An unsettled Dylan on stage
segments.body: The performances reveal a singer the reviewer describes as funny, mean, ragged and sharply focused. Dylan and the band rework songs including “Tangled Up in Blue,” “Shelter from the Storm” and “Idiot Wind,” giving them a more confrontational edge. The full concerts, the review says, make it possible to hear the flow and context that the old live album Hard Rain left out.

segments.title: A different kind of ending
segments.body: The tour’s 1976 close replaces the communal “This Land Is Your Land” ending of the previous year with “Gotta Travel On,” before a rare encore of “A Hard Rain’s A-Gonna Fall.” The review reads that change against a more uncertain political moment and sees the concert recordings as a forceful close to one phase of Dylan’s career.

content.headline: Michelle Yeoh on becoming a replicant and refusing Hollywood stereotypes
content.shortHeadline: Michelle Yeoh on Blade Runner, reinvention and refusing stereotypes
content.standfirst: The actor discusses playing a replicant in Blade Runner 2099 and the career turns that took her from ballet to Hong Kong action films and Hollywood. She also reflects on the limited roles offered to Asian actors and the films that helped shift expectations.

image.caption: Michelle Yeoh, who plays Olwen in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Life is like a heartbeat. It’s up and down, up and down’: Michelle Yeoh on casting cliches, marriage at 60 and playing a robot in Blade Runner 2099

segments.body: In Blade Runner 2099, Michelle Yeoh plays Olwen, a replicant facing a programmed end. Yeoh says she wanted the character to feel fluid rather than conventionally robotic, and built her performance around questions of what it means to be human. The series is set decades after Blade Runner 2049, in a world where replicants have power and humans occupy a subordinate position.

segments.title: A career of pivots
segments.body: Yeoh trained in ballet before a back injury forced her to reconsider that ambition. A beauty pageant led to acting work in Hong Kong, where she became known for martial-arts films. She says Hollywood later offered her stereotyped Asian roles, which she declined, before Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon and Crazy Rich Asians helped open different possibilities.

segments.title: Movement, stillness and change
segments.body: Yeoh describes herself as an actor who likes to work out a character’s physical life. She contrasts the movement of her action roles with the stillness that can make a small expression carry weight. Her account ranges from her Oscar-winning work in Everything Everywhere All at Once to the personal decisions and career reversals that shaped her path.

content.headline: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
content.shortHeadline: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman, dies aged 52
content.standfirst: The Chilean filmmaker’s death was announced by his partner, Amalia Kassai; no cause was given. Lelio’s films moved between intimate stories and political questions, including the Oscar-winning A Fantastic Woman and the internationally acclaimed Gloria.

image.caption: A still from Sebastián Lelio’s A Fantastic Woman.

sources.originalTitle: Sebastián Lelio, director of A Fantastic Woman and Gloria, dies aged 52
Sebastián Lelio was a fascinating film-maker of great passion and poetry

segments.body: Sebastián Lelio has died aged 52, according to an announcement by his partner, Amalia Kassai. She did not give a cause of death. Chilean media reported that he died at his home in Santiago. Born in Argentina, Lelio moved to Chile as a child and went on to make films in Spanish and English.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s critic places Lelio among Chile’s leading filmmakers, emphasising his ability to make stories about ordinary lives feel both sensual and political. The essay identifies A Fantastic Woman as his most accomplished work.

segments.title: Stories of desire, grief and belonging
segments.body: Lelio’s films included Gloria, about a divorced woman searching for love and meaning; Disobedience, a story of queer desire within a conservative Jewish community; and The Wonder, adapted from Emma Donoghue’s novel. His final film, the musical protest drama The Wave, premiered at Cannes in 2025.

segments.title: The impact of A Fantastic Woman
segments.body: A Fantastic Woman follows Marina, a transgender woman denied the chance to grieve after the death of her partner. It won the Oscar for best international feature, becoming the first Chilean film to do so. Lelio said its release helped revive discussion of gender identity legislation in Chile.

content.headline: Wicker’s bizarre romance invites debate about desire and devotion
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s strange romance asks what women want from men
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman and Alexander Skarsgård star in a fantasy about a husband woven from willow. The film’s deliberately skewed relationship has prompted both comic fascination and criticism over whose desires matter.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the Fisherwoman in Wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it
A husband made from a basket? Why women are going wild for freaky film romance Wicker

segments.body: In Wicker, Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a basketmaker to make her a husband, played by Alexander Skarsgård. The result is a bawdy village fantasy in which the new husband eagerly tends to his wife’s needs. The i Paper’s reviewer calls the film funny and audacious, but also questions its portrayal of a partner with little apparent agency.

perspectives.body: The BBC’s reporting on the film’s reception connects the wicker husband’s appeal to current conversations about domestic labour and the mental load in relationships. Its filmmakers say they wanted a partner who helps without expecting praise.

segments.title: The fantasy behind the jokes
segments.body: The review argues that the husband’s unquestioning devotion raises an uneasy question: can a relationship be love if one partner has no meaningful freedom? It also sees the film as a fairy tale rather than a realistic model, and finds a more serious thread in the frustration of women living under the village’s unequal expectations.

segments.title: Why the unusual lead caught on
segments.body: The BBC report describes the online response to the trailer and the film’s deliberately strange romantic premise. Writers and researchers interviewed there place Wicker within a wider tradition of human-monster romances, where outsiders and unconventional desire can challenge assumptions about beauty, power and partnership.

content.headline: Fifty years after Rocky, the underdog story still has a fresh punch
content.shortHeadline: Rocky at 50: the underdog story and how Stallone made it
content.standfirst: A cinema reissue revisits Sylvester Stallone’s 1976 boxing drama as a new film, I Play Rocky, recounts the fight to get it made. Together, the review and reporting trace the film’s blend of working-class struggle and stubborn idealism.

image.caption: Sylvester Stallone as Rocky Balboa in the 1976 film.

sources.originalTitle: Rocky review – 50 years on, Stallone’s boxer remains an exhilaratingly gritty contender
'It was a total miracle': How rejection led Sylvester Stallone to create film's ultimate underdog Rocky

segments.body: Rocky began with Sylvester Stallone, then an unknown actor struggling to find substantial roles, writing a part for himself. He refused offers to sell the screenplay unless he could play Rocky Balboa. The new film I Play Rocky dramatises that insistence and the low-budget production that followed; the original Rocky returns to cinemas for its 50th anniversary.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s review sees the original as a departure from the fatalism of earlier boxing films: Rocky loses the fight but wins a moral victory, turning a familiar tale of struggle into a rousing story of endurance.

segments.title: A gamble that paid off
segments.body: I Play Rocky’s account describes Stallone as broke and determined, even as the studio wanted an established star in the lead. Rocky was shot in 28 days on a budget of about $1m. It went on to become the biggest box-office hit of 1976, earn 10 Oscar nominations and win best picture.

segments.title: Why the story endures
segments.body: The original film follows a Philadelphia boxer offered an unlikely chance to fight heavyweight champion Apollo Creed. The review highlights its local texture and its idealistic refusal to deliver the expected betrayals. The feature on I Play Rocky argues that Stallone’s own outsider status is inseparable from the character’s appeal.

content.headline: The Social Reckoning turns Facebook’s failures into a warning about our feeds
content.shortHeadline: The Social Reckoning puts Facebook’s power back on screen
content.standfirst: Aaron Sorkin’s follow-up to The Social Network revisits reporting on Facebook’s algorithms and their effects on users. The i Paper’s review finds a chilling film whose portrait of the platform’s power is sharpened by the reviewer’s own difficulty in leaving it.

image.caption: Jeremy Strong as Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Reckoning.

sources.originalTitle: I was terrified watching The Social Reckoning – then went back to scrolling

segments.body: The Social Reckoning dramatises the reporting behind the Facebook Files, the 2021 investigation into the company’s internal research and its approach to content. The film follows reporter Jeff Horwitz, played by Jeremy Allen White, and whistleblower Frances Haugen, played by Mikey Madison, as they pursue concerns about the platform’s effects on teen mental health and political misinformation.

segments.title: A story that reaches into daily life
segments.body: The reviewer describes the film as both investigative drama and personal horror: its account of recommendation systems and outrage-driven engagement is difficult to separate from the viewer’s own use of social media. The essay’s central tension is that people may understand the harms and still feel that work, leisure and friendships depend on the same platforms.

segments.title: The reporting has moved on
segments.body: The film focuses on events that became public years ago. The review notes further controversies and the growth of Meta since the Facebook Files, while arguing that the repeated revelations have not necessarily prompted people to stop using its products. The film’s ending offers a measure of hope, but does not resolve that contradiction.

content.headline: Renate Reinsve on the role that nearly came after she quit acting
content.shortHeadline: Renate Reinsve on the film that brought her back to acting
content.standfirst: The Norwegian actor thought The Worst Person in the World might be her last film before Joachim Trier wrote a leading role for her. Reinsve reflects on the collaboration, her later work in Fjord and why she values films that leave room for audiences to decide what to feel.

sources.originalTitle: 'It stopped me quitting acting': Renate Reinsve on her life-changing role in The Worst Person in the World

segments.body: Renate Reinsve was planning to leave acting when Joachim Trier offered her the leading role in The Worst Person in the World. She says the film changed her life. Its Cannes success and her best-actress prize brought new opportunities after years in which she struggled to find screen roles she wanted.

segments.title: A character that felt familiar
segments.body: Reinsve describes Julie, the restless central character, as someone she recognised. The film follows Julie as she changes jobs and relationships while approaching 30, without presenting her choices as a simple path to certainty. Reinsve says the work felt honest because people on set found parts of themselves in the character’s contradictions.

segments.title: A different challenge in Fjord
segments.body: Reinsve’s role in Cristian Mungiu’s Fjord is markedly different: she plays Lisbet, a quiet mother whose children are taken into care after allegations of abuse. Reinsve says she wanted to understand the character without judging her. She also values the film’s refusal to tell viewers exactly what to think.

content.headline: Fourteen box-office flops that found an audience after release
content.shortHeadline: 14 film flops that deserve another look
content.standfirst: From The Thing and Dune to Babylon and Furiosa, this guide revisits films that failed commercially or were dismissed on release. Its case is that box-office disappointment does not settle a film’s value.

image.caption: A selection of films once regarded as box-office failures.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The list argues that commercial failure can obscure films worth revisiting. It ranges across genres and decades, pairing familiar misfires with later reassessments: John Carpenter’s The Thing, David Lynch’s Dune, the Coen brothers’ The Hudsucker Proxy and George Miller’s Furiosa are among the selections.

segments.title: A different reception over time
segments.body: Some entries were out of step with the moment: The Thing opened in the shadow of E.T., while Last Action Hero arrived just after Jurassic Park. Others, including Dredd and Cloud Atlas, are presented as ambitious films that struggled to find a broad audience despite their distinctive ideas.

segments.title: A recommendation, not a verdict
segments.body: The guide also includes films whose reputations have shifted, such as Heaven’s Gate and Babylon. Its argument is not that every disappointment is secretly a masterpiece, but that opening-weekend performance and later cultural life are different measures—and that a second look may reveal pleasures the first reception missed.

content.headline: The Good Daughter review: Rose Byrne leads a glossy thriller packed with trauma
content.shortHeadline: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne leads a glossy, twisty thriller
content.standfirst: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy play estranged sisters drawn back into a violent family history. The Guardian finds the opening almost comically relentless, but says the series settles into a more engaging drama when it focuses on the sisters together.

image.caption: Rose Byrne and Meghann Fahy as sisters Samantha and Charlotte in The Good Daughter.

sources.originalTitle: The Good Daughter: Rose Byrne’s legal thriller is so full of calamity it borders on Mr Bean-like farce

segments.body: The Good Daughter begins with a traumatic childhood event and quickly adds more violence, setting up a story about sisters Samantha and Charlotte Quinn. Byrne plays Samantha, a successful New York lawyer; Fahy plays Charlotte, who stayed in their Georgia hometown and became a lawyer like their father. A new crisis brings the sisters back together.

segments.title: The sisters are the strongest draw
segments.body: The review says the opening piles on so many shocks that it risks tipping into farce. The drama becomes more effective when it slows down and lets the sisters interact, including in a scene where they scramble to shut a coffin lid. Fahy, the reviewer says, holds her own opposite Byrne and gives their relationship warmth as well as tension.

segments.title: A familiar, polished thriller
segments.body: Adapted by Karin Slaughter from her novel, the series links a new murder to the family’s earlier trauma and the wider community. The review finds its plotting familiar and its presentation too polished, but suggests its broad appeal may make it a major audience draw for Byrne.

content.headline: The Assassin season two review: Keeley Hawes’s spy thriller loses its way
content.shortHeadline: The Assassin’s second season is sunk by its son’s whining
content.standfirst: Keeley Hawes returns as a midlife assassin, but the Guardian argues that her character’s relationship with her anxious adult son overwhelms the show. The review finds the thriller’s central pairing more damaging than its already convoluted plotting.

image.caption: Keeley Hawes and Freddie Highmore in The Assassin.

sources.originalTitle: The Assassin review – will anybody save Keeley Hawes from this unbearably pathetic boy?

segments.body: Season two opens with Julie Green, played by Keeley Hawes, still working as a hired killer. When her son Edward’s wife is kidnapped on honeymoon, he turns to Julie for help. The story resumes the series’ mix of family secrets, conspiracies and violent set pieces.

segments.title: A mismatch at the centre
segments.body: The review praises Hawes but finds Freddie Highmore’s Edward written as so timid and persistently alarmed that he drains the tension from the thriller. It also argues that Julie’s potential as a menopausal assassin is left largely unexplored, with her scenes too often reduced to sniping and sitcom-style bickering.

segments.title: More twists, less character
segments.body: The series continues to raise mysteries about kidnappings, past events and hidden motives, but the review regards that narrative sprawl as secondary to the central relationship. It concludes that the show’s attempt to build a long-running premise is undermined by characters who are difficult to spend time with.

content.headline: Black Doves season two review: a spy drama built on friendship and chaos
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns with implausible plots and winning chemistry
content.standfirst: Keira Knightley, Ben Whishaw and Sarah Lancashire return to Joe Barton’s espionage series. The Guardian accepts its outlandish conspiracies as part of the fun, finding its strongest thread in the friendship between Helen and Sam.

image.caption: Ben Whishaw and Keira Knightley in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Black Doves review – Ben Whishaw, Keira Knightley and Sarah Lancashire are spine-tinglingly good

segments.body: In the second season, spy Helen Webb is newly installed in No 10 while her handler, Reed, has disappeared. Helen calls on her close friend Sam, a hitman, and a collection of other assassins to help find Reed as questions gather around Helen’s cover story and the prime minister’s household.

segments.title: The cast makes the case
segments.body: The review says the show’s appeal lies less in the conspiracies than in its actors and characters. Knightley plays Helen’s social performance with precision; Whishaw gives Sam a melancholy charm, while Lancashire brings menace to Reed. Their chemistry helps the series move among espionage, comedy and farce.

segments.title: A friendship amid the mayhem
segments.body: The review notes that the show’s body count and the characters’ repeated escapes make it hard to believe in the stakes. But it finds a more grounded emotional centre in Helen and Sam’s friendship: their shared humour and loyalty offer connection amid the violence and elaborate deception.

content.headline: The Celebrity Traitors finale: Bash’s last-minute call turns the game
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors finale turns on Bash’s late suspicion
content.standfirst: After a series the reviewer found flat, the final round brings a surprise victory for the Faithful. Bash’s suspicion of Kenny—and his ability to persuade Romesh Ranganathan—changes the outcome and gives the show a late burst of tension.

image.caption: The Celebrity Traitors cast at the Endgame Round Table.

sources.originalTitle: One player’s lack of ego saved Celebrity Traitors

segments.body: The finale begins with the Traitors eliminating Michael Sheen, whom the reviewer regarded as the Faithful’s strongest hope. James Blunt then picks up Sheen’s suspicions and correctly identifies Maya Jama, who is banished at the final Round Table. The remaining Faithful, however, continue to misread the game.

segments.title: A reversal at the endgame
segments.body: Kenny appears close to winning when he chooses to end the game with several players still present. Bash realises that the decision suggests Kenny may be a Traitor and votes against him. After the vote ties with James Blunt, Bash persuades Romesh Ranganathan to change his mind; Kenny is banished and the Faithful win £83,000 for charity.

segments.title: The player who kept his head
segments.body: The reviewer credits Bash’s lack of ego for the reversal, contrasting him with players whose confidence or performance drew attention. Bash had made mistakes earlier, but the piece argues that his willingness to reconsider at the crucial moment rescued a finale—and a series—that had seemed headed for a predictable Traitor win.

content.headline: The Matthew Perry documentary review: intimate, but does it add anything?
content.shortHeadline: Matthew Perry’s Netflix documentary feels intrusive, the review argues
content.standfirst: Netflix’s three-part series revisits the Friends actor’s addiction and death, though Perry had already written about much of his experience. The i Paper’s review finds moving testimony alongside an intrusive focus on his family’s grief and little new scrutiny of the circumstances.

image.caption: Matthew Perry in a photograph accompanying the Netflix documentary review.

sources.originalTitle: Netflix’s Matthew Perry documentary is undignified and intrusive

segments.body: The One About Matthew Perry follows the actor from his early career through Friends, addiction and his death at 54 in 2023. The documentary includes archive footage and accounts from people close to him. The review notes that Perry’s 2022 memoir had already described his addiction and its effects in candid detail.

segments.title: Moving testimony, limited new reporting
segments.body: Perry’s sister describes the loneliness and pressure that accompanied his addiction, and the documentary’s archive material keeps the actor present on screen. But the review argues that the series adds little to what he said himself and moves quickly through questions about the ketamine supply and the people involved in his final months.

segments.title: The cost of access
segments.body: The critic is most troubled by the camera’s lingering attention to relatives recalling the moment they learned Perry had died. The piece asks whether the series serves viewers or the actor’s memory by revisiting that grief, and argues that Perry’s own account and his performances remain more respectful ways to remember him.

content.headline: Why Doctor Who’s future looks uncertain after its latest hiatus
content.shortHeadline: Doctor Who’s future is uncertain after the Disney+ deal ends
content.standfirst: The BBC has ended its Disney+ partnership, cancelled a planned Christmas special and put future production out to tender, with no new Doctor announced. The i Paper examines the show’s history and the questions facing its next revival.

image.caption: Several actors who have played the Doctor, including Ncuti Gatwa and Jodie Whittaker.

sources.originalTitle: The sad, slow death of Doctor Who

segments.body: Since Ncuti Gatwa’s final series as the Doctor in 2025, the BBC has ended its collaboration with Disney+ and cancelled a planned Christmas special. The corporation is seeking another partner to help fund the programme, but the report says no one has yet stepped forward and no successor to Gatwa has been announced.

segments.title: A show built on change
segments.body: The feature traces Doctor Who from its 1963 debut through its 1989 cancellation and 2005 revival. Regeneration let the series change its lead and tone, while keeping its central idea of curiosity and kindness. Fans and television historians interviewed say that renewal has been essential to the programme’s appeal.

segments.title: What went wrong—and what could return
segments.body: The article reports disagreement over the more recent scripts, the show’s audience and the value of its Disney+ deal. Some interviewees argue the latest Doctors deserved stronger material; others emphasise that the programme has survived earlier pauses. The future remains unresolved, but fans interviewed want it back on screen rather than preserved only in the archive.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into The Split’s legal-drama world
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new British Asian family
content.standfirst: The six-part spin-off moves the family-law firm from London to Manchester and centres a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creators say the aim is to retain The Split’s family melodrama while depicting characters living ordinary, contemporary lives.

image.caption: Ritu Arya and Abi Morgan at the centre of The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, played by Ritu Arya, a barrister expected to take over her family’s Manchester law firm. Her plans shift after her mother’s death alters the succession, and a former romantic partner arrives as a new colleague. As in The Split, weekly divorce cases run alongside fractures within the family.

segments.title: Representation as everyday life
segments.body: The spin-off features a predominantly British Asian cast and creative team. Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted to show a British Asian family living ordinary lives, rather than relying on the limited storylines often assigned to such characters. Arya says she researched the role by speaking with a family lawyer.

segments.title: A familiar formula with new voices
segments.body: Original-series creator Abi Morgan remains an executive producer and describes the show’s appeal as a mix of family ties, ambition and betrayal. She says the new writing team has been able to carry those themes forward while developing its own characters and stories outside London.

content.headline: 70 Up ends a landmark documentary series—and reopens its old questions
content.shortHeadline: 70 Up ends a landmark series with questions about its gaze
content.standfirst: After six decades, ITV’s Seven Up! project reaches its final chapter. The i Paper revisits the lives of its contributors and the criticisms of director Michael Apted’s framing, asking what a long-running documentary can reveal—and what it leaves out.

image.caption: Contributors to the Seven Up! documentary project when they were children.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A little pill of poison’: Why the cast of 70 Up came to resent it

segments.body: The documentary project began in 1964, following 14 children from different backgrounds and returning to them every seven years. Its final instalment, 70 Up, catches up with the surviving participants. Asif Kapadia took over directing after Michael Apted’s death in 2021.

segments.title: A portrait with blind spots
segments.body: The feature revisits participants’ objections to how the series portrayed them. Some left; others felt the programme narrowed their lives into a role or a few minutes of screen time. Jackie Basset challenged Apted’s questions about women, while John Brisby objected to being cast as the token upper-class participant.

segments.title: What a long view can—and cannot—show
segments.body: The series remains a rare record of people growing older across changing circumstances, but the article stresses that edited documentaries cannot contain a whole life. Producer Helen Houston says early childhood shapes people, while one participant reflects that there was always more to him than the programme could show.

content.headline: Titanium Court review: an 8-bit fairy game where anything can happen
content.shortHeadline: Titanium Court is a strange, surprising game worth getting lost in
content.standfirst: AP Thomson’s strategy game mixes pixel-art fairies, Shakespearean framing and optional songs about Pacific salmon. The Guardian’s critic argues that its unpredictability is not a gimmick but the point of the experience.

image.caption: A scene from the pixel-art game Titanium Court.

sources.originalTitle: Why the weirdest game of 2026 is also one of my favourites

segments.body: Titanium Court begins as a strategy game in which players match tiles and lead small fairy armies. It soon veers into strange territory: after a boss fight, a player might be offered a musical performance instead. The game’s developer, AP Thomson, wrote and recorded the music, including songs that can replace fights.

segments.title: A deliberately disorienting world
segments.body: The game’s 8-bit look, vivid pink palette and fairy-court setting frame a story full of theatrical references and unexpected digressions. Thomson says fairies gave him freedom to mix ideas, and that he wanted to move beyond familiar Tolkien-style fantasy. The reviewer argues that discovering the game’s peculiar logic is central to its appeal.

segments.title: Uncertainty as the pleasure
segments.body: The critic recommends avoiding spoilers: even after many hours, it is difficult to know what the game might do next. Its odd songs, conversations and encounters can feel startlingly personal, though Thomson says some moments emerged from combinations he had not expected players to find. It is now available on consoles and smartphones as well as PC.

content.headline: Black Tides Draga’s Wake lets a longtime games fan voice its hero
content.shortHeadline: A lifelong gamer finally voices a video-game hero
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s Dominik Diamond describes voicing Draga, a sailor in a survival-horror game made by a small, distributed team. The process turns a career-long love of games into a family memory—and a new appreciation for voice acting.

image.caption: Draga, the protagonist of Black Tides Draga’s Wake.

sources.originalTitle: After 50 years of playing video games, I’m finally starring in one

segments.body: Dominik Diamond was invited to voice the main character in Black Tides Draga’s Wake, a survival-horror game set aboard a decaying steamship after a heist goes wrong. He initially doubted that his voice suited Draga, a tough sailor infected by an ancient god, but says adjusting his performance helped it work.

segments.title: Making a game together
segments.body: Diamond describes a team spread across the world, developing the game in their spare time. The experience reminded him of bedroom programming culture and showed him the creative energy that can exist outside large publishers. The most awkward task, he says, was improvising fight noises in a garage in rural Nova Scotia.

segments.title: A family moment
segments.body: Diamond played clips for his children without telling them he was in the game. He says their reaction when they recognised their father as an action hero became one of his favourite moments as a parent. The work also made him newly attentive to the acting and direction behind video-game performances.

content.headline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans mourning a lost RPG future
content.shortHeadline: BioWare’s closure leaves Mass Effect fans with an unfinished future
content.standfirst: The Guardian’s Lucy James reflects on EA’s reported closure of the studio and cancellation of its next Mass Effect game. Her account combines the news with a personal explanation of why BioWare’s choice-driven worlds mattered to players.

image.caption: A scene from Mass Effect 3, part of BioWare’s role-playing game series.

sources.originalTitle: EA has closed BioWare – and Mass Effect fans like me are bereft

segments.body: The writer reports that EA has closed BioWare, ending a studio’s 30-year run of role-playing games, and cancelled its forthcoming Mass Effect title. The article says more than 400 people are losing their jobs. The author, a former games-industry worker and longtime fan, describes the decision as a major loss for the genre.

segments.title: A galaxy shaped by player choices
segments.body: James recalls how the Mass Effect trilogy drew her in through its characters and the decisions that carried across games. Players shaped Commander Shepard’s identity and relationships, and faced consequences for the alliances they made. The article argues that this sense of agency is central to the series’ enduring hold on its audience.

segments.title: A studio’s legacy, an uncertain sequel
segments.body: The piece acknowledges that BioWare had not produced a major critical or commercial hit in more than a decade and notes EA’s financial pressures. But it says the cancelled game had the potential to renew a much-loved universe. The closure, the writer argues, leaves western role-playing games with a smaller creative landscape.

content.headline: Baxdrostat may offer lasting blood-pressure relief for some patients
content.shortHeadline: Baxdrostat may offer lasting relief for some blood-pressure patients
content.standfirst: A small follow-up analysis found that some patients’ blood pressure stayed lower after they stopped taking the drug. Researchers say larger studies are needed before it can be called a lasting cure.

sources.originalTitle: New drug that could permanently cure high blood pressure coming to UK by 2027

segments.body: A follow-up analysis of a larger baxdrostat trial found that 14 patients with substantial blood-pressure reductions continued to have lower readings after stopping the drug. Their treatment lasted six to 12 months; the reported follow-up extends to two years, with one patient followed for three years.

segments.title: A finding that needs testing
segments.body: The researchers think the drug may have killed aldosterone-producing cells in small adrenal tumours, which can cause high blood pressure. But the proposed mechanism and lasting benefit are not established: the analysis involved a small group, and a larger study is under way. Baxdrostat’s approval in the US is for difficult-to-control high blood pressure, not a proven permanent cure.

content.headline: Lightning may change as the climate warms, with consequences for fires
content.shortHeadline: How a warming climate could change lightning and fire risk
content.standfirst: Lightning helps shape ecosystems, but changing storm conditions could also increase dangerous ignitions. Research suggests possible shifts, especially at higher latitudes, though projections vary widely.

image.caption: Lightning flashes across a storm-darkened sky.

sources.originalTitle: Thunderstruck: what does the future hold for lightning?

segments.body: Lightning is not only a hazard: it contributes to the nitrogen cycle and helps shape fire-dependent ecosystems. But a warming climate may change where and how often it strikes. A review of studies, still under peer review, found projections ranging from an 11% decrease to a 44% increase in lightning per degree of warming, with an average projected increase of 7.5%.

segments.title: Fire and uncertainty
segments.body: Researchers see broad agreement that lightning will increase at high latitudes, but are less certain about tropical regions. Dry lightning can ignite remote fires that are difficult to reach; the article cites Australian records showing 50% more dry-lightning strikes in south-eastern forests in 2000–16 than in the previous two decades. Lightning alone does not determine fire severity: dryness, heat and wind also matter.

content.headline: Scientists link enjoyable conversations to a balance of focus and fresh ideas
content.shortHeadline: Study links better conversations to a balance of focus and novelty
content.standfirst: In analyses of conversations between strangers, friends and speed-dating pairs, exchanges with a particular pattern of shifting between topics were linked to greater enjoyment and connection.

image.caption: Two people talk during a conversation.

sources.originalTitle: Want to have a better chat? Scientists say the secret is ‘pink noise’

segments.body: Researchers analysed more than 1,000 conversations between strangers, as well as chats between friends and speed-dating pairs. People tended to report more enjoyment and connection when conversations showed what the researchers call “pink noise”: staying with a subject long enough to explore it, then bringing in fresh ideas rather than becoming stuck or jumping randomly between topics.

segments.title: A pattern, not a recipe
segments.body: The team used an AI system to score each turn for meaning, tone and context, then assessed how the conversation changed over time. Pink noise was associated with enjoyment and, in speed-dating chats, predicting which pairs met again. The study does not establish that a conversational technique causes better relationships; a conversation analyst also cautioned that judging exchanges mainly by enjoyment can miss the importance of difficult or emotionally significant conversations.

content.headline: Was Verica, the Iron Age ruler who drew Rome to Britain, a queen?
content.shortHeadline: Was Verica, the ruler linked to Rome’s invasion, a queen?
content.standfirst: An archaeologist argues that coin designs and inscriptions could point to a female ruler, but other specialists say the evidence is inconclusive and some details may support a male reading.

sources.originalTitle: Historians say King Verica persuaded Rome to invade Britain. But could Verica actually have been a queen?

segments.body: Archaeologist Miles Russell argues that Verica, an Iron Age ruler who fled to Rome before the invasion of Britain in AD43, may have been a woman. His case draws on the name’s ending, the word “Rex” on coins, images that he interprets as feminine and inscriptions that he says could mean “daughter of” rather than “son of”.

segments.title: A disputed interpretation
segments.body: Other specialists quoted in the report say the evidence does not settle Verica’s sex. Roger Tomlin notes that some male Latin names end in “a” and says Russell has not shown that “Rex” was used for women as well as men. Coin expert Daphne Nash Briggs points to coins bearing apparently male figures; Russell disputes those readings. The theory remains a proposal, not an established historical conclusion.

content.headline: US prosecutors drop charges against Harvard scientist Kseniia Petrova
content.shortHeadline: US drops charges against Harvard scientist Kseniia Petrova
content.standfirst: Federal prosecutors have dismissed the case against the Russian scientist, who spent four months in immigration detention after arriving with frog-embryo samples for research. The reasons given focus on the government’s priorities and resources.

image.caption: Kseniia Petrova leaves a federal courthouse in Boston.

sources.originalTitle: US prosecutors drop criminal charges against scientist detained over frog embryos

segments.body: US prosecutors have dropped all criminal charges against Kseniia Petrova, a Harvard Medical School scientist who was arrested after returning from France with frog-embryo samples intended for research. The charges included smuggling, concealing facts and making false statements. A federal judge granted prosecutors’ request to dismiss the case.

segments.title: A disputed prosecution
segments.body: Prosecutors said the costs of continuing the case outweighed the public interest in resolving it, while describing Petrova’s claims of vindictive and selective prosecution as meritless. Her lawyer criticised the decision to bring charges; the Department of Homeland Security had maintained that she lied to federal officers. The report says Petrova had spent four months in immigration detention and feared deportation to Russia.

content.headline: SpaceX’s Starlink Mobile aims to become a US carrier, but the buildout is costly
content.shortHeadline: Starlink Mobile’s US carrier ambitions face a costly buildout
content.standfirst: SpaceX plans to combine satellite-to-phone service with a terrestrial mobile network, including spectrum and cell sites. The head of T-Mobile’s parent company says the project could require at least $200bn.

sources.originalTitle: Starlink Mobile: All the news on SpaceX’s major mobile carrier ambitions
T-Mobile owner on Elon Musk launching a wireless carrier: ‘Welcome to the party’

segments.body: SpaceX says it wants Starlink Mobile to compete with major US carriers by combining direct-to-cell satellites with a ground-based network. The plans described include acquiring low-band spectrum and using Qualcomm technology at tens of thousands of 5G sites, with deployments expected from 2027. SpaceX has also reportedly discussed access to cell towers and a possible deal involving Boost Mobile.

segments.title: The cost of competing
segments.body: Deutsche Telekom chief executive Tim Höttges, whose company owns T-Mobile, said SpaceX’s ambitions should be taken seriously but estimated that spectrum and network construction could require at least $200bn. That is his assessment, not a confirmed project budget. SpaceX’s plans remain dependent on building or accessing the terrestrial infrastructure as well as expanding satellite service.

perspectives.body: Höttges argues that spectrum is only part of the expense: SpaceX would also need towers and antennas to compete with established mobile networks. He sees a potential new kind of communications service, but says it will not come cheaply.

content.headline: TikTok videos may funnel young viewers toward adult-content platforms, study say
content.shortHeadline: Study says TikTok videos can steer young users toward adult content
content.standfirst: Researchers from two campaigning organisations say creators use coded references in lifestyle videos to promote paid sexual content elsewhere. TikTok and OnlyFans say they have rules and safeguards against sexual content and underage access.

image.caption: A person uses a phone displaying TikTok.

sources.originalTitle: TikTok accused of helping to promote sex industry to girls

segments.body: A report by UK and Australian campaigning organisations says some popular OnlyFans performers use TikTok lifestyle posts to hint at explicit material sold elsewhere. Researchers cite coded terms, emojis and links between accounts, alongside videos presenting paid sexual content as a route to wealth. The material they studied was non-explicit; the report argues that it can still promote the adult-content industry to young audiences.

segments.title: Platforms’ responses
segments.body: The researchers call for restrictions on under-18s seeing not only pornography but also posts that promote or relate to the sex industry. TikTok says it prohibits sexual content and uses technology to enforce its rules, including safeguards intended to keep age-inappropriate material from teens. OnlyFans says its service is for adults and that it has onboarding checks to prevent minors from accessing it.

content.headline: Philadelphia professor’s protests challenge sidewalk delivery robots
content.shortHeadline: A professor is blocking delivery robots to protest their use on city
content.standfirst: Carolyn Marvin says delivery robots do not belong in public space and argues that residents should have a say. The protest has drawn supporters and criticism, and she is contesting a disorderly-conduct ticket.

image.caption: Carolyn Marvin blocks a delivery robot during a protest in Philadelphia.

sources.originalTitle: Standing in the way of slop bowls: the woman blocking food delivery robots

segments.body: Carolyn Marvin, a semi-retired University of Pennsylvania professor, has repeatedly stood in front of Uber Eats delivery robots in Philadelphia to protest their presence on sidewalks. Police issued her a disorderly-conduct ticket after one confrontation; she says she will challenge it and invokes her right to protest in public space.

segments.title: Who are sidewalks for?
segments.body: Marvin argues that the robots may take jobs and create hazards for people with mobility issues, and says residents should have a say in whether private machines use public streets. Reactions are mixed: some passers-by support her, while others worry about interrupting deliveries. Pennsylvania law treats delivery robots as pedestrians, and the operator Avride says making the machines seem approachable helps people feel comfortable around them.

content.headline: South-east Asia reins in data-centre boom as power and water constraints mount
content.shortHeadline: Power and water pressures slow south-east Asia’s data-centre rush
content.standfirst: Thailand paused projects and Indonesia halted one development as governments and communities weigh resource demands. The region remains a major growth hub, but new approvals are increasingly tied to energy and water requirements.

image.caption: A data centre stands within a residential area in Thailand.

sources.originalTitle: The datacentre arms race hits pause in south-east Asia

segments.body: South-east Asia’s data-centre expansion is running into limits on power, water and planning. Thailand paused construction on 49 projects and decisions on 117 more in September, while authorities in Indonesia’s West Java halted a development over permits and an incomplete environmental assessment. The region has a large share of Asia-Pacific capacity under construction, much of it in Malaysia and Thailand.

segments.title: Who bears the costs?
segments.body: Wood Mackenzie estimates that data centres already use 24% of the power consumed in Malaysia’s Johor state, a share that could reach 40% by 2035. Water needs are also a concern in drought-prone Johor and in parts of Thailand where reservoirs are under strain. Governments are tightening approval frameworks, while an academic quoted in the report questions whether communities receive benefits proportionate to the infrastructure and environmental costs.

content.headline: DataVita drops direct-renewables claim for Scottish AI data-centre plan
content.shortHeadline: Scottish AI data-centre plan now relies on the National Grid
content.standfirst: DataVita has revised its plan for a Lanarkshire project, saying the site will be grid-served and that wind and solar could connect later. The change raises questions about earlier claims of direct renewable supply.

image.caption: The existing DataVita data centre at Chapelhall, near Airdrie.

sources.originalTitle: Lanarkshire AI datacentre to fully rely on National Grid despite renewables claim

segments.body: DataVita now says its proposed data centres near Chapelhall, Lanarkshire, will be “fully grid served”, with wind and solar projects potentially connected in future. That differs from an earlier claim that more than 1GW of renewable capacity would be delivered through private connections to the site.

segments.title: The company’s explanation
segments.body: DataVita says its commitment to renewable energy is unchanged and that grid power would be covered by a renewable power-purchase agreement. The report notes that the company has public wealth guarantees and that its project has been promoted as part of the UK’s AI strategy. An environmental campaigner quoted by the Guardian describes the shift as emblematic of exaggerated claims by data-centre developers.

content.headline: Google takes over troubled Wyoming data-centre project from Crusoe
content.shortHeadline: Google takes over an unfinished Wyoming data-centre project
content.standfirst: Crusoe has sold an unfinished site to Google, which plans to invest $17bn in its development. The handover highlights the difficulty of securing power, equipment and schedules for very large AI infrastructure projects.

sources.originalTitle: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google

segments.body: Data-centre developer Crusoe has sold an unfinished project in south-eastern Wyoming to Google, which announced plans to invest $17bn in the campus. Crusoe had previously sought Google as a customer for the project.
